Welcome to my blog. Alongside the papers listed under
[Research](../../../ResearchProjects.qmd), I wanted a place for the ideas *around*
the work — the methods, the intuitions, and the open questions that rarely fit
into a manuscript. This first post explains why I find this field so compelling.

## The map of disease is being redrawn

For most of the twentieth century, the geography of many infectious diseases felt
fixed: dengue was tropical, West Nile virus was a concern for warmer latitudes, and
temperate Europe was largely spared. That assumption no longer holds. Warming
temperatures, changing rainfall, expanding vector habitats, and the sheer volume of
human mobility are pushing pathogens into places that were previously unsuitable —
and doing so faster than historical intuition would predict.

In our recent work, the interval between the establishment of *Aedes albopictus* in
a European region and its first local outbreak of dengue or chikungunya fell from
around 25 years to under five over the last three decades. That is not a gradual
drift; it is an acceleration.

## Why data science, and not just epidemiology

Understanding this shift requires more than surveillance. It requires models that
can absorb heterogeneous data — climate reanalysis, land cover, socioeconomic
indicators, mobility networks — and separate signal from noise across space and
time. Three ideas guide how I approach it:

- **Prediction with explanation.** A model that forecasts outbreaks is useful; a
  model that also tells us *why* a region is at risk is actionable. Explainable AI
  lets us do both.
- **Mechanism where it matters.** Machine learning captures complex patterns, but
  process-based models encode what we know about transmission. The most trustworthy
  answers usually come from combining the two.
- **Spatial diffusion, not just suitability.** Eco-climatic suitability explains
  *where* a disease could spread; diffusion dynamics explain *why some suitable
  places are invaded and others are not*. Both are needed.

## What I'll write about here

Expect posts on the methods I use and the reasoning behind them — survival and
time-to-event analysis, ecological niche modelling, the pitfalls of disease risk
mapping — as well as broader reflections on climate, health, and the craft of
turning messy data into decisions. Some will be technical; some will be short notes.
